chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Fazzal, from Thal'abah ibn Maymoun, from Yahya ibn Zakariyya, from Abu Ubaydah who said:

I was a travel companion of Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), and I used to begin with mounting (the animal), then he (peace be upon him) would mount. So when we were both settled, he (peace be upon him) would greet and ask questions like a man who had no prior pact with his companion, and shake hands. He (the narrator) said, 'And it was so that whenever we descended, he (peace be upon him) descended before me. So when I and he were both established upon the ground, he (peace be upon him) would greet and ask questions like the one who had no pact with his companion.' So I said, 'O son of the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him)! You are doing something which no one has done before us, and if you were to do it once, so it would be a lot.' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'Do you not know what is in the handshake? The two believers meet, so one of them shakes the hand of his companion, so the sins do not cease to fall from them both just as the leaves fall from the tree, and Allah (exalted is He) looks at it (the handshake) until they both separate.'
ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual benefit of shaking hands between two Muslims according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the etiquette of greeting, noting that he would initiate the handshake to demonstrate its spiritual efficacy rather than out of mere social custom. He reveals that the physical act of *muṣāfaha* serves as a mechanism for the expiation of minor sins, likening their shedding to leaves falling from a tree, a concept deeply rooted in Shia jurisprudence regarding the sanctity of social bonds. This practice underscores the belief that physical interactions between believers are not merely social but are charged with divine mercy and spiritual purification.
